newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech leaders discuss new government declaration. [CORRECTED 21:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Czech leaders discuss new government declaration. [CORRECTED 21:35 GMT]

text.p: Leaders of the three parties in Czech republic's (corrects from Czechoslavakia) ruling centre-right coalition began discussions on Tuesday on a declaration to accompany expected changes in the cabinet, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said.
Klaus said he would push for a rapid reconstruction of the cabinet to try to end the political uncertainty which has caused a sharp fall in the Czech crown in recent weeks.
The crown lost about eight percent of its value on Tuesday after speculators' attacks forced the central bank on Monday to allow it to float.
Currency traders said they were anxiously following the coalition talks to give support to the crown or allow it to fall further.

Klaus told journalists as the evening talks began that party chairmen hoped to present a joint statement about the coalition's governing programme to the broader party leaderships for approval later on Tuesday.

Senior government officials said they expected coalition leaders to meet again on Wednesday and brief journalists on the talks before Klaus leaves around midday for a ceremony on the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan in the Netherlands.
Talks between the parties in the centre-right coalition ended inconclusively on Monday, two days after the finance, industry and trade, and interior ministers tendered their resignations.

The leaders agreed to change the cabinet last week in order to answer a sharp drop in the centre-right government's approval ratings following an economic downturn and a widespread feeling that financial crime is pervasive.
But Monday's meeting suggested a final agreement on the share-out of ministerial posts would be difficult.

After meeting the coalition leaders on Tuesday, President Vaclav Havel said he believed the current coalition should continue ruling the country, but that they needed to agree quickly on how to move forward.

"With the chairmen we agreed that it would be the best if now... leaderships of these parties... began working on something which would clearly articulate which aims this government has, how it wants to come to terms with the current economic situation," Havel told a news conference.

"That means accompanying measures to yesterday's floating of the exchange rate of the crown, what long-term aims it has on the background of which it wants to act in short-term, what concepts it has got in various areas of its activity."
He said personnel changes should be an expression of the new course, and hinted that if the coalition could not reach agreement, the whole government should step down.

"If the coalition partners don't agree, if these negotiations fail... to formulate something which will give the hope, certainty to citizens, which will show the way out of this situation... then nothing would be left but to hope for other solutions - you probably know what I mean," Havel said.
